title: Auth administration-retention check is quadratic in grant count

history.note: Ran the repro (bench:auth:record, exit 0) on a fresh checkout. Fresh means: retention 10 top 0.00007953ms, 100 top 0.00047393ms, 10 bottom 0.00380715ms, 100 bottom 0.42786674ms. Headline spread 5380x (task said 5187x). The discriminating test held: a 10x grant increase costs 112.4x on the bottom arm vs 5.96x on the top arm, so growth is superlinear only when administrationReachable cannot exit early. Mechanism confirmed at the sites: auth-v1.ts:443 does grants.some() with a full evaluateGrantStack per candidate, auth.ts:321 and :349 call it on every REMOVE_GRANT and MOVE_GRANT. Note the cost is bounded by MAX_AUTH_GRANTS=100, so the worst legal price is 0.43ms of CPU per auth write, not unbounded.

Replaced administrationReachable's per-candidate evaluateGrantStack (O(n^2)) with a single reverse pass that shadows decided addresses, in packages/shared/document-model/auth-v1.ts; the boolean is unchanged (220k-trial differential against the HEAD implementation, 0 divergences), so this is an implementation change to a v1 consensus rule and needs no policy version bump. Retention at 100 grants administered from the bottom went from 0.4132 ms to 1.4902e-4 ms; the 10->100 growth on that arm went from 109.89x to 1.00x and the headline spread against 10-grants-from-the-top from 5395x to 2.76x, while the from-the-top arm also improved (100-top 4.6460e-4 -> 2.3808e-4 ms) and the 'evaluateGrantStack: 100 grants (cap), match last' control held at 0.979x. bench:fix compare against a criterion written before the edit: MET, exit 0. Tests: shared 218 pass, document-model 392 pass, reactor 2998 pass with Postgres variants run, lint clean. Coverage gap from the independent verify run (bench:fix ci, 8/8 steps exit 0): 'Steps 7a (reactor lint / test:reactor with Postgres) and step 8 (--integration) did not fire because the diff never touches packages/reactor/**. So although Postgres is reachable on 5433, no PG-backed test variant actually ran in this invocation - the reactor-suite/Postgres path only activates for reactor-path changes, and this diff is in packages/shared. This is a correct scoping decision by ci, not a gap it hid, but it means PG variants ran is not something I can claim for this run.' Also not run by ci: full pnpm build, storybook build, pnpm test:integration, browser-project suites outside test:ci related. The reactor suite with PG reachable was run by the fixer, not by the CI mirror.

details.observed: In auth policy evaluation (pure CPU) > auth scope write validation, retention: 100 grants, administered from the bottom is 5187.43x slower than retention: 10 grants, administered from the top; going from 10 to 100 grants administered from the bottom (a 10x increase in grant count) costs 108x more time (0.00393ms mean to 0.42384ms mean), while the same 10x increase administered from the top costs only 5.96x more (0.0000817ms to 0.0004866ms)
details.expected: Retention cost should scale linearly with grant count, as the administered-from-the-top case does, not quadratically. administrationReachable's some() walks every grant that could be an administration candidate and, for each one, calls evaluateGrantStack, itself an O(n) full-stack scan because last-applicable-grant-wins forbids early exit. When every earlier candidate is shadowed by a later deny, installable and not synthetic per the fixture comment at bench/fixtures/auth-policies.ts:273-284, this becomes one O(n) evaluateGrantStack call per candidate, i.e. O(n^2) total, and this check runs on every REMOVE_GRANT or MOVE_GRANT write to the auth scope
details.magnitude: 5187.43x recorded spread; O(n) vs O(n^2) scaling confirmed by the 108x-vs-5.96x growth ratio at a 10x grant count increase

fixes.summary: Determine administration reachability in a single pass over the grant stack, tracking the last-applicable grant per administration-capable subject while scanning once, instead of one full evaluateGrantStack call per candidate grant
fixes.expectedEffect: Retention check becomes O(n) regardless of where the surviving administration grant sits in the stack

fixes.summary: Cache the evaluateGrantStack decision for the full grant stack once per assertAuthAdministrationRetained call and reuse it across administration candidates where the decision does not depend on subject-specific evaluation
fixes.expectedEffect: Removes the per-candidate re-scan without restructuring the reachability algorithm

title: Group principal membership check is an uncapped linear scan with per-member lowercasing

history.note: Ran the repro (bench:auth:record, exit 0). The numbers reproduce: group of 10 members 0.00025742ms, group of 1000 0.00853261ms, group absent 0.00015612ms, so 54.7x against absent (task said 55.41x) and 33.2x for a 100x member increase (task said 33.1x), and auth-v1.ts:852 is indeed group.members.some with a per-member toLowerCase. What fails is the claim the finding rests on. The title says uncapped and the expected says no corresponding cap on group member count exists and the cost is unbounded as rosters grow. A cap exists: MAX_GROUP_MEMBERS = 1000 in packages/reactor-group/document-models/reactor-group/v1/src/reducers/group.ts:12, enforced in addMemberOperation at :50, and the groups projection the evaluator reads (packages/reactor/src/decision/auth-decision-model.ts) is built from those PHGroup documents. So the bench's largest case is already sitting exactly at the cap: 0.0085ms is the worst legal price, not an unbounded one, and the marginal cost is 8.4ns per member. That is the same situation as MAX_AUTH_GRANTS = 100, which the task itself cites as the reason grants are acceptable. The finding is technically true only under its own narrow scoping to packages/shared/document-model, where no cap is expressed; the type carries no bound but the write path does. The Set-of-lowercased-addresses fix is still a valid micro-optimization worth about 8.4us at the cap, but it is not the uncapped unbounded scan filed. Refile against the real cost if wanted: 8.5us per grant that names a full 1000-member group.

details.observed: In auth policy evaluation (pure CPU) > group principals, 10 grants, group of 1000 members is 55.41x slower than 10 grants, group absent from the map; against the group of 10 members case, a 100x increase in member count costs 33.1x more time (0.000274ms mean to 0.009073ms mean)
details.expected: Group membership matching should not cost more as a group grows, or at least should not require an unbounded scan: unlike grants, which the model caps at MAX_AUTH_GRANTS, no corresponding cap on group member count exists anywhere in packages/shared/document-model. principalMatches resolves a group principal with group.members.some, calling member.toLowerCase() on every element until a match or exhaustion, so every grant that names a group re-pays this scan and the cost is unbounded as rosters grow
details.magnitude: 55.41x recorded spread; near-linear growth with member count (33.1x time for 100x members) and no upper bound on member count in the type

fixes.summary: Normalize and cache group membership as a Set of lowercased addresses once when the groups projection is built, and look up membership by Set.has instead of Array.some with per-member toLowerCase
fixes.expectedEffect: Membership check becomes O(1) per grant regardless of roster size

title: Mixed and error-aggregation event-bus benches hide subscriber waits inside the label

history.note: Sites confirmed verbatim: event-bus.bench.ts:40 is the setImmediate await in createMixedSubscriber, :352 is the unconditional setTimeout 1ms in createAsyncErrorSubscriber, and EventBus.emit at src/events/event-bus.ts:51-57 awaits subscribers sequentially. Bias demonstrated by A/B on the real EventBus: my copy of the filed mixed subscriber reproduces the recorded 50-subscriber 50/50 mean at 0.3669ms vs 0.3611 recorded, and swapping only the async branch to a microtask drops it to 0.0034ms, 108x. Marginal cost per async hit is 14.5us vs 45-48ns for a microtask subscriber, the roughly 300x the task claims. Conclusion 3 reproduces at 24.22x with setImmediate and collapses to 4.33x on microtask, so about 82 percent of that headline is macrotask scheduling. Error aggregation async reproduces at 3.867ms with the sleep and falls to 0.0088ms without it, so 99.8 percent is timer. One correction: the task says 2 of 3 subscribers sleep, but createAsyncErrorSubscriber sleeps unconditionally so all 3 do, which makes the bias larger than filed, roughly 3 times 1.15ms against a 3.49ms mean rather than 2.3ms.

Remedy applied as filed. createMixedSubscriber's async branch and createAsyncErrorSubscriber both resolve on a microtask now; the setImmediate hop survives as one labelled case, 50 subscribers (50% sync, 50% yield to macrotask via setImmediate). Criterion written before the run: holds if 50/50/50 falls well under 0.02ms and error aggregation (async) under 0.05ms; fails if Mixed means stay near 0.0144ms times n times p. Run of vitest bench --run bench/event-bus, exit 0: 50 subscribers 50/50 0.0034ms against 0.358ms in B-005, the labelled macrotask case 0.359ms, error aggregation (async) 0.0038ms against 3.85ms. Re-record events to replace B-002/B-005.

details.defect: createMixedSubscriber's async branch awaits new Promise(resolve => setImmediate(resolve)) (a macrotask) instead of the microtask-resolving pattern used by createAsyncSubscriber's 0ms path. Across all seven Mixed-suite cases, mean divided by (subscriberCount times asyncProbability) is approximately 0.0144ms regardless of n or p (range 0.01403-0.01495), meaning the suite is entirely pricing count-of-setImmediate-hits, not sync/async ratio or dispatch overhead. A real microtask-resolving async subscriber costs roughly 45-48ns marginal (from the Async Emission Throughput suite's 5-to-10-subscriber deltas at 0ms delay), so setImmediate hits cost roughly 300x more per subscriber than a representative async subscriber -- the Mixed suite's headline conclusion #3 (50 subscribers 50/50 is 24.15x slower than 10 subscribers 90/10) is an artifact of this ~300x-inflated per-subscriber cost, not of ratio or count. Separately, createAsyncErrorSubscriber unconditionally awaits setTimeout(resolve, 1) before the error check; with 2 of 3 subscribers taking this path under sequential emit, 2 times approximately 1.15ms (the Async suite's own 1-subscriber/1ms-delay mean) accounts for roughly 2.3ms of the observed 3.49ms mean for Error aggregation (async) -- headline conclusion #5 (573.13x slower than sync) is almost entirely the baked-in 1ms sleep, not error-aggregation cost. Both suites hide the wait inside the subscriber body instead of naming it in the case label, unlike the Async Emission Throughput suite which names delays explicitly and is caveated for low sample counts on exactly those cases.
details.remedy: Rebuild the Mixed suite's async branch on a microtask-resolving delay (matching createAsyncSubscriber's 0ms path) so it measures dispatch/ratio cost, not macrotask-scheduling cost; if an I/O-yielding scenario is wanted, keep setImmediate but give it its own labeled case rather than folding it into the sync/async ratio sweep. Rebuild createAsyncErrorSubscriber without the unconditional 1ms sleep (or name the delay in the case title) so Error aggregation (async) prices error-path cost rather than timer cost. Conclusions #3 and #5 in B-002 should be treated as artifacts; the Sync Emission, plain Async Emission, and Subscription Management suites are unaffected.

title: Two-reactor sync scenarios time setup and polling scaffolding, not just convergence

history.note: Sites confirmed: two-reactor-sync.ts:284-285, 313-314, 344-345 and 373-374 call connectDocuments and createDocuments inside run; :211-243 polls with 2 getOperations per document per cycle plus a 25ms sleep; :246 assertConverged does a get plus JSON.stringify per document; bench.add at :493 passes scenario.run as fn with lifecycle as FnOptions; tinybench 2.9.0 dist/index.js:277-287 samples now after beforeEach, so beforeEach is untimed and run is the whole timed window. Bias measured with an instrumented copy of the harness, one pass per scenario, run totals matching the record: Baseline 892.4ms vs 885.5 recorded, Conflicts 1285.5 vs 1313.4, Heavy Load 29121.8 and 29805.0 vs 32026.7. Scaffolding inside the timed region, excluding the 25ms sleeps so convergence wait is not counted against it: Baseline 59.6 percent of run, Conflicts 53.8, Heavy Load 47.8 and 48.1. The composition shifts with document count exactly as claimed: connect plus create is 21.8 percent of Baseline but 2.9 percent of Heavy Load, while the polling reads are 20 reads costing 324.7ms at Baseline against 100 reads costing 12646ms at Heavy Load. Caution for the remedy: moving connect and create is not neutral. Wrapping those three calls in a pass-through async timer, which only adds a microtask hop before the first writes, made Deep Hierarchy stall past the 60s timeout 3 of 3 runs while the unmodified harness converged in 1.1 to 1.26s 3 of 3.

Correcting a run count in my previous note; verdict unchanged. The Deep Hierarchy caution should read: wrapping connectDocuments, createDocuments and assertConverged in a pass-through async timer, which only adds a microtask hop before the first writes, made Deep Hierarchy stall past the 60s timeout in 3 of 3 instrumented runs plus a fourth run of a variant carrying only those wrappers, while the unmodified harness converged in 2 of 2 runs I made, 1.1s under bench:sync:smoke and 1.257s under an uninstrumented driver. Everything else in the previous note stands: sites confirmed, tinybench 2.9.0 times only fn, and scaffolding inside the timed window is 59.6 percent at Baseline, 53.8 at Conflicts, 47.8 and 48.1 at Heavy Load, with connect plus create falling from 21.8 percent of Baseline to 2.9 percent of Heavy Load and polling reads rising from 20 reads at 324.7ms to 100 reads at 12646ms.

Remedy applied as filed, plus one site the task did not name: settle() polled getJobStatus every 5ms per write inside the window. connectDocuments, createDocuments and the creates' own convergence moved to beforeEach; assertConverged to afterEach; the 25ms poll replaced by a JOB_READ_READY/JOB_FAILED tracker that reads the logs once per document per side only after every tracked action id has been indexed on both sides. Case names now end in (writes to convergence) so the series is not confused with B-003/B-008. Four consecutive smoke runs 4/4. Baseline 0.72s timed vs 0.885s recorded, which is the setup share; the polling reads overlapped sync rather than extending it, so Heavy Load moved 30.3s to 29.0s. Re-record sync to replace B-003/B-008.

details.defect: Each scenario's run function is the timed tinybench fn (tinybench 2.9.0 times only fn itself; beforeEach/afterEach in FnOptions run outside the timed window, confirmed in node_modules/.pnpm/tinybench@2.9.0/node_modules/tinybench/dist/index.js around the loop() method, and lifecycle.beforeEach there only calls setupTwoReactors, which is untimed). But connectDocuments and createDocuments -- the per-document syncManager.add calls and the sequential awaited creates -- are called inside run(), at lines 284-285 (Baseline), 313-314 (Conflicts), 344-345 (Heavy Load), and 373-374 (Deep Hierarchy), so they sit inside the timed region along with the writes. waitForSync (lines 211-243) then polls every 25ms, doing 2 getOperations reads per document per cycle against the same pglite instances the executors are still writing to, and assertConverged (lines 246-258) does a full reactor.get plus JSON.stringify per document. All four pieces of scaffolding scale with document count (10 in Baseline, 50 in Heavy Load), so the fraction of each case's wall time spent on setup/polling/verification rather than on sync itself differs across cases, and the polling reads add I/O contention that competes with the writes being measured.
details.remedy: Move connectDocuments and createDocuments into lifecycle.beforeEach (already untimed by tinybench) so run() times only the writes plus convergence. Replace waitForSync's 25ms polling loop with an event-driven wait (e.g. resolving on the JOB_READ_READY events already emitted per job, one per side) so the timed region stops issuing reads that scale with document count. Keep assertConverged, or move it out of the timed window if only sync latency is wanted, and say which was chosen in the case title.

title: No isolated measurement of cross-reactor same-document write contention

history.note: Searched bench/ for a harness answering the question. Nothing measures cross-reactor same-document contention: reshuffle appears nowhere under bench/ except in this task, two-reactor-sync.ts has no scenario matched to Baseline doc count that alternates the writer per op, Conflicts is 5 docs against Baseline 10 and Deep Hierarchy changes action type, and nothing separates queue wait from apply time. Ran the nearest existing harness, vitest bench --run bench/queue-only, exit 0: Queue Profiling Extensions / conflicting operations on same document drains 180 same-document jobs in 0.086 to 0.091ms of dequeue time, 0.2162ms mean for the whole case at 2313 samples. That is in-memory InMemoryQueue mechanics only, with synthetic jobs, one process, no executor, no sync-load jobs and no reshuffle, so it does not answer the question. It does bound one candidate out: queue bookkeeping CPU is about 0.1ms per 180 same-doc jobs, three orders of magnitude below the roughly 400ms Conflicts-minus-Baseline gap, so whatever the gap is it is waiting and apply work, not queue data-structure cost. dequeueNext fairness under contention in queue-perf.bench.ts is round-robin fairness across 80 documents and is not closer. Gap stands; note it is blockedBy T-004, whose scaffolding share of 48 to 60 percent of the timed window must come out before the 45-48 percent gap itself can be trusted as a sync number.

The measurement exists and has run as B-012. Contention is Baseline with only the writer alternating per operation: 10 documents, 10 setDriveName each, same creator split. Every case now attributes its jobs from the lifecycle events into local writes, plain loads and loads that re-appended already-written operations (reshuffles), with per-job queue wait, apply and index means in the record's derived list. What B-012 shows, for the analyst to read: Contention 956ms against Baseline 682ms, a 40 percent gap at matched document count and action type, so the Conflicts and Deep Hierarchy gaps were mostly contention rather than their confounds. Every one of Contention's 28 non-empty loads reshuffled (157 ops re-appended per iteration) where Baseline's 28 loads reshuffled none. Per job, reshuffle apply (36ms) is close to plain load apply (43ms) and local queue wait is lower under Contention (65ms) than Baseline (72ms); the number that moves is index time, 504ms per reshuffling load against 142ms per plain load, and local index at 273 to 323ms dominates local apply at 29 to 50ms in every case. Two limits: per-job means are not wall time, since jobs on different documents overlap, and 2 of 5000 Heavy Load writes lacked a complete stamp set per iteration and were skipped.

details.question: At equal total write-operation counts, Baseline (10 docs times 10 ops, one reactor writes each doc) has a mean of 885.5ms while Conflicts (5 docs times 20 ops, writers alternate reactor per op on the same doc) has a mean of 1313.4ms and Deep Hierarchy (10 docs times 5 levels times 2 actions, folder from reactor A and file from reactor B interleaved per doc) has a mean of 1284.1ms -- roughly 45-48 percent higher than Baseline for the same op count. How much of that gap is queue serialization forcing local writes to wait behind incoming sync-load jobs for the same document (queue.ts enforces per-document serial execution across scopes and branches), how much is the reshuffleByTimestamp/reshuffleByTimestampAndIndex tie-breaking path for concurrent operations, and how much is confounded by Deep Hierarchy using different action types (addFolder/addFile) than Baseline's setDriveName?
details.experiment: Add a scenario matched to Baseline's op count and document count that alternates the writing reactor per operation on the same document (isolating cross-reactor contention from doc-count and action-type confounds), instrument or log queue wait time versus reduce/apply time per job, and record whether reshuffle is invoked and how often across the two reactors for that scenario.
details.whyItMatters: If most of the 45-48 percent gap is queue serialization waiting on sync-load jobs, that is an inherent cost of the documented per-document serialization invariant and not fixable without relaxing it. If it is instead dominated by reshuffle's tie-breaking work, that scales with conflicting-operation count and is a candidate for optimization. Without isolating the mechanism, B-003's Conflicts and Deep Hierarchy numbers cannot be used to reason about where cross-reactor contention cost comes from, only that it exists.

title: Queue hot-path bench cases loop unequal job counts, so per-case hz is not cost-per-job

history.note: Ran bench:queue:record (exit 0). Op counts at the four cited sites are as claimed (40,000 enqueues / 2,000+2,000 / 600+600 / 1,200x3). Fresh meanMs divided by op count: retry churn 0.466 us/op, dequeueNext 0.549, bulk enqueue 0.550, dependency scan 1.762 - so dependency scan is the most expensive path per op at 3.2x the next case while sitting at hz rank 2, and the per-op spread is 3.78x against the recorded 12.8x. Two corrections: the task's 0.29 us/op for retry churn needs 6,000 ops while its prose counts 3,600 (0.466 at 3,600, same ranking), and 'inverted' overstates it - retry churn is rank 1 under both accountings, the real content is dependency scan moving from rank 2 to slowest. A PH_BENCH_VERBOSE=1 run confirms the parenthetical about vitest timing the whole callback: dependency scan's internal drain window is 0.31ms of its 2.11ms mean, so its per-op cost lives in the 600 reverse-ordered enqueues, not the dequeues.

T-006's harness bias is removed by giving every queue-perf case the same 3,600 queue-operation budget derived from one OPS_PER_CASE constant (bulk 200x18, dequeueNext 72x25, dependency scan 3 chains of the preserved 600, retry 1200x3), so per-case hz is now cost-per-job. Criterion written before the edit (scratchpad/criterion.json @ 2026-09-04T13:43:48.140Z: bulk enqueue mean <= 0.12x of 22.7878 ms, missed at >= 0.20x, control retry loop churn within +/-15%): bulk enqueue 22.7878 -> 1.1770 ms (0.052x), control retry 1.6753 -> 1.7304 ms (1.033x), bench:fix compare verdict MET (exit 0); dependency scan moved from hz rank 2 to slowest (2.0557 -> 6.1410 ms, hz 486.45 -> 162.84) and the recorded rank-1/rank-4 spread fell from 13.60x to 5.22x. PARTIAL: the pre-written spread band of <=5.0x missed by 4.4% because the 3.78x per-op target was itself computed across unequal batch sizes (bulk enqueue costs 0.57 us/op at 40,000 jobs but 0.33 at 3,600); the dep-scan-over-retry pair landed at 3.55x. OPS_PER_CASE was deliberately not retuned to fit the band. Reactor tests pass (185 files / 2998 tests, exit 0, Postgres variants executed against 5433) and tsc --noEmit is clean. COVERAGE GAP: lint did not inspect the changed file - eslint exited 0 with a 0-byte log because **/*.bench.ts is ignored at root eslint.config.js:76 (TODO 'investigate why our benchmark tests fail so many lint checks'), so step 6's pass means 'no matched files to lint', not 'lint approved the diff', and lint-staged parity cannot be verified for this file. Also not run: full pnpm build, storybook build, browser-project suites outside test:ci related, pnpm test:integration. NOTE FOR THE NEXT RECORD: B-006 is now a non-comparable baseline, not merely outdated - its means were measured at 40,000/4,000/1,200/3,600 ops while future queue records measure 3,600 each, so the after-fix record should supersede B-006; the equalized budget also retires B-006's 'bulk enqueue: 23 samples, too few' caveat (n=425, rme 1.65%), but its expect()-in-the-timed-callback caveat still applies to all four cases.

details.defect: Each case's timed callback (vitest bench times the whole callback, not just the internal hrtime t0/t1 window, which only feeds PH_BENCH_VERBOSE logging) drives a different number of queue operations: bulk enqueue does 200x200=40,000 enqueues, dequeueNext fairness does 80x25=2,000 enqueue+dequeue/complete pairs, dependency scan does 600 enqueue+dequeue/complete pairs, and retry loop churn does 1,200 enqueue + 1,200 dequeue/retry + 1,200 dequeue/complete (3,600 ops). B-006's own question is 'What does the queue cost per job at realistic batch sizes?' but neither the per-case hz/meanMs nor the derived 'spread' (rank-1 hz over rank-4 hz, reported as retry loop churn being 12.8x faster than bulk enqueue, restated in conclusions[0]) divides by op count. Normalizing meanMs by each case's queue-op count instead gives roughly 0.56 us/op (bulk enqueue), 0.54 us/op (dequeueNext fairness), 1.8 us/op (dependency scan), 0.29 us/op (retry loop churn): the true per-op ranking is inverted relative to the recorded hz ranking (dependency scan is the most expensive path per op, at rank 2 of 4 by raw hz, not the slowest).
details.remedy: Equalize the number of queue operations looped per case (same documents x jobsPerDoc / chainLength / totalJobs), or have the record divide meanMs by a per-case opCount so hz and the derived spread represent cost-per-job as B-006's question asks, instead of cost-per-invocation of loops of differing size.

title: Write-cache rebuild recomputes a full state hash per replayed op instead of reusing the stored one

history.note: Ran the repro verbatim (pnpm bench:cache:record, exit 0): cold miss rebuild 16.2751ms at 100 ops vs 854.2752ms at 1000 ops = 52.5x for a 10x op increase, no-cache manual rebuild 60.4x, keyframe-resume/coldMiss100 = 0.684 - the observed superlinearity, not the expected O(operations). A first run agreed within noise (53.1x, 0.676). Code confirms the mechanism at both sites: reducer.ts:639 computes hashDocumentStateForScope unconditionally and kysely-write-cache.ts:966 passes only skip/protocolVersion. Three numbers the record lacks: (1) the hash is 44.5% of a 1000-op replay and 24.2% at 100 ops, scaling 98x for 10x ops against the total's 53x - the steepest-growing component but not the only O(state) one, so removing it alone will not linearize rebuild; (2) fix rank 1 as written is inert - reducer.ts:639-644 computes the hash and only then overwrites it from replayOptions, and passing replayOptions:{operation} changed a 1000-op replay by +0.9%; (3) only fix rank 2, or moving the hash under the replayOptions check, avoids the work.

Criterion, set before the after-run: cold-miss 1000-op rebuild mean <= 0.65x the before-run, and hashDocumentStateForScope no longer reachable on the replay path. baseReducer computed a full scope-state hash on every operation and then unconditionally discarded it in favour of the stored one; the hash is now computed only when the replayed operation carries none, and coldMissRebuild/warmMissRebuild pass replayOptions:{operation} (with skipIndexValidation:true, since keyframes are persisted with operations:{} and the contiguity check replayOptions introduces would reject the first resumed op). Cold-miss rebuild at 1000 ops went 856.86ms -> 463.82ms (0.541x, -45.9%, threshold 556.96ms), at 100 ops 17.24 -> 11.66ms, warm-miss 50-op 19.43 -> 15.81ms; the untouched no-cache control held at 857.96 -> 833.51ms (0.971x). The 45.9% removed corroborates the verifier's measured 44.5% hash share. Reducer output is bit-identical for every input: the old 'hash !== ""' guard is subsumed by a truthy check, and the site was an overwrite, not a verify - nothing ever compared the computed hash to the stored one, so no safety property was removed and fix rank 2 (a new opt-out flag for an already-dead computation) was unnecessary. Note the verifier's warning held: fix rank 1 as written is inert (+0.9%), because the compute had to be made lazy as well as fed. Tests green: shared 218 pass, document-model 392 pass, reactor 2958 pass in 179 files, lint 0 errors. Independent verify agent: green, no coverage gap - typecheck, root lint on both files, circular-imports, check-ts-references, full test:ci matrix, pnpm test:reactor (2958/2958, Postgres reachable on 5433 and the PG-backed variants executed, zero skips), and test:integration (load-test-connect + hub-spoke-catchup) all exit 0. One unrelated red on the first test:ci run was root-caused to a stale packages/reactor-api/dist predating commit aa0f1e93a, not to this diff. RESIDUAL, not fixed here: cold-miss rebuild is still superlinear (100->1000 is 39.8x, vs 52.5x before) - removing the hash changed the constant, not the shape. keyframe-resume/coldMiss100 moved only 0.661 -> 0.666, which rules out an O(history) term such as the per-op operations-array copy and points at O(state)-per-op work; the analyst candidate is the mutative create() draft in baseReducer. Deserves its own task.

details.observed: Cold miss rebuild scales worse than the operation count: 100 ops means 16.76ms, 1000 ops means 877.13ms (rme 0.50-1.43%, so the means are trustworthy even though the 10-sample caveat flags the derived spread) - a 52x cost for a 10x increase in operations. The no-cache manual-rebuild baseline, which never touches kysely-write-cache.ts and shares only module.reducer with the cached path, shows the same shape (14.19ms at 100 ops to 865.15ms at 1000 ops, ~61x for 10x), so the superlinearity lives inside the reducer, not in cache bookkeeping. The keyframe-resume case (replaying 49 ops from revision 50) costs 11.20ms versus 16.76ms for replaying 100 ops from scratch - a 0.67x ratio that tracks accumulated state size (nodes 51..99 vs 1..100, ~0.73x) far better than remaining operations-history length (~0.24x, which is what a per-op array-copy of document.operations[scope] would predict). _baseReducer calls hashDocumentStateForScope(newDocument, scope) - which stringifies and hashes the entire scope state - unconditionally on every applied operation, before checking whether options.replayOptions?.operation.hash could be reused. kysely-write-cache.ts's rebuild loop never sets replayOptions, so every operation replayed during a cold or warm miss pays a full state-size hash even though the correct hash for that operation is already sitting in the OperationStore.
details.expected: Replaying operations that were already validated and hashed on write should cost O(operations), not O(operations x accumulated state size). Both do per-batch work: SubscriptionNotificationReadModel.indexOperations at subs/subscription-notification-read-model.ts:22 loops every operation classifying action types, and ProcessorManager extends BaseReadModel with commitOperations at processor-manager.ts:86 calling detectAndRegisterNewDrives, detectAndCleanupDeletedDrives and routeOperationsToProcessors, after which BaseReadModel.indexOperations at base-read-model.ts:66-74 runs an unconditional db.transaction().execute for any non-empty batch. Grep counts: zero reads of event.postReadyDurationMs anywhere under bench, the only hits being the prose of this task and T-009; zero occurrences of the string postReady in BENCHMARKS.jsonl. Ran pnpm bench:sync:smoke, exit 0, all 5 scenarios passed: every attribution line prints exactly wait, apply, index and chain wait, so the shipped harness cannot show a post-ready duration, as predicted. Its index means reproduce B-015, Baseline local index 39.767ms with chain wait 317.5918ms against B-015's 41.16 and 327.96, Heavy Load local 145.2671ms with 14080.4168ms against 147.41 and 15038.83, confirming the bucket measured is the one B-015 reports. Magnitude of the omission measured on an instrumented scratchpad copy, shipped file untouched, git status shows only TASKS.jsonl modified; pre-registered thresholds MATERIAL at 15 percent of the index bucket and IMMATERIAL below 5 percent; two runs, both exit 0, both all 5 scenarios passed. Local per indexed job, run 1 then run 2: Baseline postReady 28.2338 and 29.0241ms against index 39.5659 and 41.4283ms, so 71 and 70 percent; Heavy Load postReady 140.1323 and 148.1397ms against index 148.4523 and 157.4477ms, so 94 percent both times; Heavy Load load-side postReady 505.7688ms against index 1107.3524ms, 46 percent. So the omitted phase is 70 to 94 percent of the number the record reports as index, and the omitted fraction grows with load, 0.71 to 0.94 of index from Baseline to Heavy Load while postReady itself grows 4.96x against index's 3.75x, which answers the task's second question in the affirmative. This also reproduces T-009's unrecorded 26 to 139 ms/job almost exactly at 28.2 to 140.1. Nearest existing measurement named and why it does not refute: T-009's VERIFIED history note, which is a task-history note taken on an instrumented copy of B-012's pre-fix code, not a script and not a B-id; the GAP rule is to name the script or the B-id, and neither exists. The numbers above are a scratchpad instrumented copy, not a harness and not a record, so the GAP stands until the fourth bucket lands in the shipped bench and a record carries it.

details.question: B-015's derived "index" bucket (bench/two-reactor-sync.ts:303, stamp.indexMs += event.preReadyDurationMs + event.emitDurationMs) intentionally excludes postReadyDurationMs, per T-009's verified correction that JOB_READ_READY already fires before the post-ready stage runs. But postReady is not bookkeeping: the default coordinator two-reactor-sync.ts builds (no coordinator override, so ReactorBuilder falls through to src/core/reactor-builder.ts:882-884) runs subscriptionNotificationReadModel and processorManager as postReady, and both do real per-batch work -- subscription-notification-read-model.ts's indexOperations (line 21 on) loops every operation classifying action types and firing relationship-change callbacks, and processor-manager.ts's commitOperations (line 86) plus BaseReadModel.indexOperations's unconditional db.transaction().execute(saveState) (base-read-model.ts:59-71) issue a real PGlite write every batch. T-009's own verifier measured this stage on an instrumented copy of B-012 at 26-139ms/job, the same order of magnitude as B-015's reported "index" means (41.16ms Baseline local, 147.41ms Heavy Load local). How much read-model cost is B-015's (and B-021's) "index" bucket omitting, and does the omitted fraction grow with load the way chain wait does?
details.experiment: Instrument two-reactor-sync.ts's READMODEL_BATCH_COMPLETED subscriber (coordinator.ts:200-203 already carries postReadyDurationMs on the event; the bench subscriber at two-reactor-sync.ts:298-303 just does not read it) to accumulate event.postReadyDurationMs into a fourth bucket per scenario, alongside queue wait/apply/index/chain wait, and record it as its own derived series so postReady cost is visible in BENCHMARKS.jsonl instead of only in a verifier's scratch note.
details.whyItMatters: Every sync record since the T-009 fix (B-015, B-021) reports "index" as if it were total read-model indexing cost, but it is only the pre-ready phase; the phase that keeps GraphQL subscriptions and installed processors current runs after JOB_READ_READY and is invisible to every derived number in the record. Anyone using these "index" means to reason about total read-model CPU/DB cost per operation is working from a figure that is, by T-009's own unrecorded measurement, roughly half the real cost -- and nothing says whether that gap is constant or grows with scenario load the way chain wait does.

title: Drive reducer's node sort mutates through the mutative draft proxy at roughly a 10x per-node tax, and it is what survives T-016's fix

history.note: Reran the record repro as vitest bench --run bench/write-cache with outputJson sent to the scratchpad instead of bench/results, exit 0. Fresh draft-leg per-node wall slopes: full 0.8191, no reads 0.5390, no sort 0.4992, push only 0.0019 us/node. Sort-comparator bucket is 0.3199 us/node on the draft against 0.0337 on the plain leg, a 9.5x per-node tax where the task predicted about 10x. What survives removing the read scans from the draft is 65.8 percent against the predicted about 65, and the read scan is 34.2 percent of the wall slope and 38.3 percent of the mirror body slope against the predicted about 35 and about 39, so T-016 removing about 92 percent does not hold. Removing the reads outright is more generous than routing them through current, so 65.8 percent is a lower bound on what T-016 leaves. Decomposition sanity checks pass: plain-leg touch term is 0.0006 us/node at 1.0 percent of full, and mirror/real slope fidelity is 0.9944x draft and 0.9947x plain. node.ts:46 in addFileOperation and :82 in addFolderOperation are both a full Array.prototype.sort over the draft on every ADD_FILE and ADD_FOLDER at HEAD 86d1c7d35.

tags: case:Write Cache Cold Miss Replay Read/Write Split

details.observed: B-023's Write Cache Cold Miss Replay Read/Write Split suite isolates the sort as its own bucket, distinct from T-016's read-only find/collision scans. At the 100-op draft-leg row, all non-caveated with sample counts 208/307/306/2265 and rme under 0.4 percent: reads plus push plus sort means 4.826ms, push plus sort (no reads) means 3.266ms, reads plus push (no sort) means 3.273ms, push only means 0.442ms. Sort and reads each cost about 1.55ms of the 4.38ms non-push-only body, i.e. removing either one alone saves about the same amount. At the 2000-op draft-leg row, sample count 10 for the three slower variants with rme at or under 1.3 percent, so the caveat about few samples applies but the pairwise differences here are 40 percent or more of each case mean and survive it: reads plus push plus sort 1692.04ms, push plus sort 1129.63ms so reads cost about 562ms, reads plus push 1041.48ms so sort costs about 650ms, push only 11.86ms. The plain-leg control at 2000 ops shows the same shape at far smaller magnitude: reads plus push plus sort 116.26ms, push plus sort 67.22ms so reads cost about 49ms, reads plus push 50.81ms so sort costs about 16ms. Per-node, plain-leg sort is roughly 0.033 microseconds per node against roughly 0.32 microseconds per node on the draft leg, a tax of similar shape and magnitude to T-016's 12.5x read-scan tax, but the mechanism is different: node.ts:46 and :82 run state.nodes.sort with a comparator that reads a.id and b.id every comparison, and sort is a write through the draft that mutative must copy-on-write, not a read-only scan. The bucket is not cleanly additive with the read scan: whichever statement touches an element first pays for that element's child-draft creation, so once T-016's fix routes the find and collision-scan reads through current or original, the sort becomes the first statement to touch each element and inherits the touch cost the reads no longer pay. Net effect on T-016: its rank-1 and rank-2 fixes only remove the read-scan share of the per-node tax, about 35 percent of the per-node wall slope and about 39 percent of the body slope per B-023's case means, not the roughly 92 percent originally claimed in T-016's fixes. The sort, plus the touch cost it now solely owns, is the roughly 65 percent that survives both ranked fixes.
details.expected: Sorting the node array inside a reducer running on a mutative draft should cost close to the same per element as sorting a plain array, since the comparator only reads two id strings per comparison and does not need to mutate anything; instead the comparator's element reads through the draft proxy carry a per-node tax an order of magnitude above the plain-state equivalent.
details.magnitude: roughly 10x per-node tax for the sort alone at the 2000-op row, draft about 0.32 microseconds per node vs plain about 0.033 microseconds per node; corrects T-016's fix expectation of removing about 92 percent of the tax down to about 35 percent

fixes.summary: Compute the correct insertion index for the new node from ids read via current() or original() and splice the node into place once, avoiding a full sort() over the draft so the comparator never runs against the proxy
fixes.expectedEffect: Removes the sort's per-node tax, about 0.32 microseconds per node at these sizes, in addition to whatever T-016's fix already removes from the read scans

fixes.summary: Read the node array via current() or original() into a plain array, sort that plain copy, and assign it back to state.nodes once per operation
fixes.expectedEffect: Same removal of the sort's per-node tax as rank 1, at the cost of one extra full-array copy per operation instead of a single splice

title: No-cache baseline replay recomputes a whole-scope-state hash per op that both production replay paths skip

history.note: Code claim confirmed at HEAD 86d1c7d35: write-cache.bench.ts:701 calls state.module.reducer with two arguments only, reducer.ts:639-642 falls to hashDocumentStateForScope when replayOptions is absent, and kysely-write-cache.ts:973 and :1282 plus simple-job-executor.ts:868 all pass replayOptions. The seeded stored ops do carry a hash, appendOperations sets hash documentId-hash-index, so the remedy is live rather than inert. Discriminated by copying the bench to an untracked sibling with only replayOptions operation storedOp added at :701, running the No-Cache suite isolated before and after, both exit 0, then deleting the sibling. Before: 14.4485ms against 12.3737ms at 100 ops is 1.168x, 815.42ms against 467.27ms at 1000 ops is 1.745x, so the widening factor is 1.494, matching B-023 at 1.51. After: 9.4894ms against 11.2026ms at 100 ops is 0.847x, 437.03ms against 456.04ms at 1000 ops is 0.958x, widening factor 1.131, inside the pre-registered 1.2 threshold. The baseline leg alone fell 378ms at 1000 ops, 46 percent, while the with-cache control moved 2.4 percent, so the hash recompute fully accounts for the widening and the pair reads about 1x once it is removed. Overestimate bias on the No-cache baseline cases of B-007, B-020, B-022 and B-023 confirmed.

details.defect: measureManualRebuild calls state.module.reducer(document, storedOp.action) with only two arguments, so the reducer's options parameter is its default empty object and options.replayOptions is undefined for every replayed op. At reducer.ts line 639 to 642, replayHash is only taken from options.replayOptions, operation, hash; when it is undefined the else branch runs hashDocumentStateForScope(newDocument, scope), an O(nodes) hash over the whole scope state, on every single replayed op. Both production replay paths that this bench function is meant to stand in for do pass replayOptions with the same stored operation object and so reuse its already-known hash instead of recomputing it: kysely-write-cache.ts line 973 and line 1282 call the reducer with replayOptions colon operation colon operation inside the write cache's own cold-miss rebuild, and simple-job-executor.ts line 868 does the same with replayOptions colon operation colon sourceOperation. The stored operations that measureManualRebuild reads at write-cache.bench.ts line 686 to 699 via state.fixture.store.getSince are the identical stored-operation objects the production paths pass as replayOptions.operation, so the hash is available to measureManualRebuild and simply is not passed. Confirmed identical code at HEAD and at B-007, B-020 and B-022's recorded reactorShas, so this is not new to B-023. The record side shows the shape an O(nodes) recompute would produce: in B-023, No-cache baseline: manual rebuild is 13.979ms at 100 ops versus With cache: rebuild at 11.788ms, a 1.19x ratio, widening to 852.836ms versus 474.906ms at 1000 ops, a 1.80x ratio, a tenfold increase in op count producing near-quadratic rather than linear growth in the gap. The same widening appears in B-020, 1.19x at 100 ops to 1.73x at 1000 ops, and B-022, 1.16x at 100 ops to 1.77x at 1000 ops. B-007's pair is noisier, 0.88x at 100 ops and 0.98x at 1000 ops, but the code is identical so the same bias is present there even where sampling noise obscures it. This widening is not explained by the existing caveat that the pair reads about 1x by construction, since that caveat covers a fixed-size comparison, not why the ratio itself grows with op count. The No-cache baseline cases pay a per-op hash-recompute cost that the With cache leg's own internal cold-miss rebuild does not pay, on top of whatever the cache genuinely saves.
details.remedy: Pass replayOptions colon operation colon storedOp, mirroring kysely-write-cache.ts line 973, in measureManualRebuild's call to state.module.reducer, so the manual baseline pays the same replay cost model as the production paths it represents. This isolates whatever the write cache genuinely saves from an incidental hash-recompute artifact of the bench's own baseline function.
